newsitem.title: UK: Dollar finds firm footing in calmer Europe.
newsitem.headline: Dollar finds firm footing in calmer Europe.

text.p: The dollar got a firm foothold above 1.54 marks and 113 yen in Europe as stock and bond markets steadied after a bout of year-end profit-taking and as European Union leaders moved closer to agreement on a budgetary stability pact this weekend.
European finance ministers meet at 1600 GMT to prepare for the weekend summit in Dublin.
Chartists were bullish for a dollar move above 1.55 marks later on Thursday, while economists were keeping a close eye November U.S. retail sales and consumer price reports, due at 1330 GMT.
"The comments we've been seeing throughout the morning make it more likely that we will see agreement on a stability pact at the weekend," said Teis Knuthsen, economist at First Chicago.
"It's still uncertain what kind of pact we're going to get but a weaker deal than the hardline German stance would be dollar positive against Europe," he said.
EU leaders said today they were hopeful of a deal.
At 1204 GMT, the dollar was trading at 1.5460/65 marks, up almost one pfennig from the close here Wednesday at 1.5370/75. Against the yen, it was at 113.19/29 compared with 112.77/82 late yesterday.

"The market has become very optimistic over the prospects of a stability pact at the forthcoming summit," said Avinash Persaud, head of currency research at JP Morgan in Europe, referring in particular to recent movements of interest rate spreads in the swaps market.

German Chancellor Helmut Kohl told parliament today he was confident of an agreement on the stability pact and said monetary union should start on time. A spokeswoman for French president Jacques Chirac said there was good hopes for a deal.
A return to EMU optimism without a hardline German stance would weigh on the mark across the borad, analysts said.

"Mark strength overnight reflected risks of a "no pact' scenario but we now assume a compromise will be reached by necessity and will be positive for the peripheral European EMU candidates," said Joe Prendergast, foreign exchange strategist at Merrill Lynch. "A pact would enhance the chances that the periphery could be included in an early EMU group."

The dollar was given a further lift as French calls for a higher dollar against the new single currency were backed up by the European Monetary Institute president Alexandre Lamfalussy. He said the dollar was undervalued against European currencies, while intra European parities were now correct.
